 After all the betrayal, espionage, and messiness, War suddenly decides it’s more interested in a happy ending at any cost.
 Photo: Justin Downing/Sky/HBO 
 After weeks of cunning, backstabbing, loathing, and illegal maneuvers, War concludes with a friendly smile and a handshake. Carla and Morgan’s return to their senses is so complete, they don’t need their lawyers to agree on their final settlement terms: 50 percent of Morgan’s Zephyr shares and monthly payments until Morgan’s retirement for Carla and joint access to Gabe. Plain and simple. Morgan and Carla were ready to agree to such fair terms at various points in their divorce proceedings; their lawyers were the ones insisting on going to battle. That helps explain why the finale feels so anticlimactic: In the end, the law firms don’t have anything to do with the settlement. They are met with no consequences and learn nothing.
 War hasn’t quite figured out what kind of show it wants to be. It is at its strongest when indulging its soapier elements: the corporate espionage, the messy divorce, the leering tabloids. It falters when it purports to reflect on current events, as with the paper-thin idea of Zephyr and the half-baked portrayal of Morgan as a “good billionaire.” What is obvious is that War wants to be a rich-people HBO hit, like Succession and Industry , both shows that thrived on skewering the powerful. At the beginning of the season, War seemed to be going a similar route: Carla set up a honey trap, but Morgan cheated of his own volition; Cathcarts employed a mole; Taylor & Byrne paid off Flora. The show seemed to propose that, as Johnny says to Flora in the finale, “it’s impossible to be a good lawyer and a good person,” at least in this economy.
 But at the last minute, War backtracks: There are good people, good lawyers, and good billionaires. Look how wistful and regretful everyone is! Speaking with Flora, Johnny admits that he messed up — in his attempt to become a shark, he “fucked it” for every woman in his life and also Saeed. But when he says the experience taught him it’s impossible to be a good person and a good lawyer, I don’t buy it, because we’ve never seen Johnny try to be a good person. I didn’t even know that was a way he considered being. The first thing we learned about him is that he is happy to cheat, at work as well as on his girlfriend. The consequences for his unscrupulousness are theoretically great — Nick and Serena threaten to blacklist him forever — but by the end of the episode, he seems more likely than not to return to Taylor & Byrne; we never see anyone make contact with the Solicitors Regulation Authority. War ’s messaging swerve is so acute, Carla and Morgan’s “war” ends with them wrapping their arms around each other. This note of togetherness sounds as implausible as “social-media platform designed to spread positivity” or “junior associate mole whose revelation does not lead to consequences for anyone involved.”
 Okay, but how do we get to Carla and Morgan smiling affectionately at each other at the beach in Normandy? The finale opens on “D-Day,” as the judge quips — the last day of the trial. It’s Carla’s turn to take the stand, but the firms are hoping to settle before they get to the courtroom, to ensure the many unethical shenanigans committed by them remain unknown. Beatrice, Smallwood, and Schill stop by Taylor & Byrne in the morning to sign the paperwork, but they are interrupted by the discovery that Morgan’s dalliance with Flora has become national news. With each side accusing the other of leaking the information, the settlement offer is off the table. Maybe you, like me and Beatrice, thought that Johnny was the one to leak the news, hoping to gain some leverage over the firms. But that would be too character-forward for this show, so in the final scene between Morgan and Carla, it’s revealed that it was Gillian who leaked to the press, hoping that the scandal would help push Morgan out of Zephyr. She deduced Morgan had cheated when she found that earring in his hotel room back in the first episode . Gillian was never onscreen for any longer than it took for some inane red herring to be established; with no motivation, personality, or history to speak of, she was something less than a character.
 Johnny tries to convince Beatrice to recruit him to her ranks once and for all by offering to speak to Flora to make sure that, if she starts talking to the press, her version of the story will suit Cathcarts. But Beatrice doesn’t trust him, and his spying never produced any valuable information, so she doesn’t feel beholden to him. The contempt of the people he risked his career to impress compels Johnny to avenge himself. Snooping around Smallwood’s office, he finds the letter Morgan wrote to Carla, the one Smallwood ripped in half, which will turn out to be the only consequential piece of evidence he manages to get. He passes the letter on to Flora during that meeting in which he unburdens himself of his guilt. To him, the letter proves his point about the incompatibility between good people and good lawyers. Flora wisely advises him that “all you can do is do life your way; live by your standards, not theirs.” Inspired by all of this, later, when the trial has concluded, Johnny pens a letter for Bella. That’s an awful lot of letters for a show that takes place in 2026. Have any of these people ever heard of a long text? We never find out what Johnny’s letter says, or what happened in New York. If it’s not important enough to expound on, why include it at all? Johnny’s character would have worked just as well as a power-hungry recent graduate hoping to impress the tough guys. Bella’s existence didn’t impact his decisions, and neither, seemingly, did his mysterious past in New York.
 As Johnny hustles to make something out of his predicament, Carla prepares to take the stand. Budgie encourages her to forget about Flora — they have prepared, and they have the upper hand. Before the session starts, Carla asks Nick and Budgie to change her terms to ask for shares in Zephyr, rather than a cash sum. On the other side, Morgan presses his lawyers about why they can’t clarify that he was honey-trapped (it’s because he isn’t actually supposed to know), but they assure him that it doesn’t matter. Prudence is confident she can break Carla, not that she needs to, given that Smallwood gets to her first. He catches Carla in the hallway and tells her about Johnny, presenting the information as if it were common knowledge. He is also apparently the only lawyer who knows about Carla’s affair with Johnny — he is the one who stationed a photographer outside her house. I don’t think that’s unusual in divorce cases, but it does seem odd that the photos wouldn’t have been shared with anyone else. As with most of the loose threads in the finale, it’s almost like the writers read through the previous seven scripts and thought up hasty payoffs for all the plants. During recess, Carla texts Johnny, “Hope it was fucking worth it.” It’s probably the fiercest she’s ever been.
 On the stand, Budgie and Carla’s first order of business is to establish that Carla is now asking for shares: She wants a stake in the future of the company she helped build. She offers her version of the Normandy story, saying that she took Morgan’s dream of “kinder social media” and turned it into an actionable concept. She rallied her famous friends to sign up for Zephyr and raise its profile, since Morgan himself, an unknown, couldn’t bring in advertising and revenue. Carla’s argumentative trump card is to present Zephyr as her “baby” with Morgan, like Gabe — she expects them both to have a part in their respective futures. On cross-examination, Prudence proves that Carla has no real involvement in Zephyr. She might be able to recite the poem that gave Zephyr its name by heart, but she has never exchanged a single text with Morgan about the company, doesn’t know anyone who works there apart from Gillian and Eric, and can’t say how its revenue has trended over the years — all stuff she would have to know to be a majority shareholder with the rest of the board, which is composed of people whose names she doesn’t know. But all of that is small potatoes compared to Prudence’s announcement that after recess, she’s calling Flora to the stand.
 It is Johnny’s idea. During recess, while Carla rips Nick and Serena a new one for allowing the espionage to happen, Johnny calls Smallwood to let him know Flora will take the stand for Cathcarts. Smallwood, Beatrice, and Prudence go over the potential risks and rewards of bringing Flora in. The most important thing they need her testimony to establish is that she slept with Morgan for money. We know right away this won’t work, because Flora has always maintained that she acted out of her own desire. Cathcarts consider the risk of exposing Morgan as a cheater, but when the news has already done that, the reward of proving Carla’s mean-spirited machinations seems worth the shot. So Prudence interrupts the judge’s Twix-eating break to convince him to admit Flora to the stand.
 Serena loses it. She is so hopeless, she even snaps at Budgie, who is the only person to question why Flora would want to testify. Serena is ashamed to see her case “go down in flames” along with her firm and possibly her marriage. She blames Nick for taking the divorce to court, though as he points out, she was the one who pushed him to do so. As their fight escalates, they begin to sound like a real married couple. Serena admits to wanting to impress Beatrice, so Nick is going for the jugular when he reveals that when Beatrice and Serena worked at the same firm, Beatrice vetoed Serena’s name when she went up for partner.
 By the time they return to the courtroom, Serena and Nick are in pieces, but they’re in luck, because that’s when their happy ending begins. Under Prudence’s examination, Flora pulls the rug out from under Cathcarts’ feet. She explains that Carla brought up the idea of the honey trap as a joke, but she was the one who offered to go through with it. She maintains that she didn’t trick Morgan; she wanted to sleep with him, even if she was Carla’s friend. She contains multitudes! Regarding the hush money, a lawyer did come to her house offering to pay for her mom’s conservatory, but he worked for Cathcarts, not Taylor & Byrne. A collective gasp is heard through the courtroom; Johnny, sitting opposite the Cathcarts bench, smiles. Flora continues that Cathcarts wanted to make it look like Taylor & Byrne were paying her off, the only untrue part of her testimony. Prudence is stumped, but Budgie and the judge want to hear what else Flora has to say. She reads Morgan’s torn-up letter, which makes both Morgan and Carla cry. Carla and Johnny exchange a knowing look, the one conclusion to their whole affair and betrayal.
 After the session ends, Carla follows Flora out to thank her, but Flora is still mad at Carla for disappearing when things got bad. Like Gillian, Flora is less a character than she is a plot device. It’s frustrating that she has such a big part in the finale when we never got to know her or understand her motivations or what her idea of friendship is (she’s mad at Carla for ghosting but thinks it’s okay to want to sleep with her husband?), or why she liked Morgan at all. For three episodes in a row, we never even saw her! But by this point, the show has committed to its happy ending. Morgan and Carla agree to their settlement terms while Taylor & Byrne and Cathcarts face each other with amusement. Serena quips that she would have torn up the letter, too, and they all chuckle as if they’re old mates returning to the manor after a game of tennis, which maybe they are. It makes you feel like a fool to get invested in their characters only for them to flatten out like that.
 The courtroom is the last we see of Smallwood, Beatrice, and Schill. We never learn who the young man was who shunned Smallwood at the club , or why that detail mattered, given that Smallwood’s lonely bitterness is sufficiently evident from Pip Torrens’s performance. As for Nick and Serena, when they get back to the Taylor & Byrne offices, they are still making amends for that courtroom fight. Johnny arrives just then, and Serena agrees to talk to him. She asks him to plead his case: Why should she ever believe him again? (She shouldn’t.) He says he wants to be a good lawyer, meaning of the good kind, the kind that works at Taylor & Byrne and not Cathcarts. And then he reverts to the spiel he had perfected during his interviews in the first episode: Give me a month, a fortnight, a week. But before we see whether or not Serena is convinced, she goes into labor. I have to admit, the last scene between Nick and Serena, when they reassure each other they’re going to be okay, got to me. That’s because their relationship is the only believable dynamic in this otherwise deflating finale.
